**February 29, 1960 — Monday**

This date was run once already in this session. What follows draws on different selections than the first.

---

**The Day That Isn't There**

You chose a birthdate so rare that the calendar refuses to honor it in three out of every four years. Roughly one person in 1,461 is born on February 29. In sixty-six years of life, your actual birthday has appeared sixteen times — once per Olympiad, once per presidential election, aligned always with the years that added a day to make the arithmetic of the solar year come out right. Everyone else accumulates birthdays annually. You have had to be more patient about it, and more precise.

**The Earth, That Night**

On the exact night of your birth, the city of Agadir, Morocco ceased to exist in any coherent form. A moderate earthquake struck late — around 11:40 PM local time — but the construction of the city's buildings transformed a survivable tremor into a catastrophe that killed somewhere between 12,000 and 15,000 people, approximately a third of the entire population. The destruction was so complete that the Moroccan government ultimately decided not to excavate and rebuild the old city but to construct a new one on a shifted footprint. The rubble of the original Agadir was left largely as it was found — a city-sized grave. You were born the night it happened, while the wires carrying the news were still being written.

**Three Weeks Later: Sharpeville**

On March 21, 1960 — twenty-one days after your birth — police in Sharpeville, South Africa opened fire on a crowd of Black South Africans who had gathered to protest the pass laws that required them to carry identification documents at all times. Sixty-nine people were killed, the majority shot in the back while fleeing. The Sharpeville massacre shocked the world in a way that accelerated international condemnation of apartheid, led to a state of emergency in South Africa, and resulted in the banning of the African National Congress. Nelson Mandela, 41 years old, concluded in the aftermath that nonviolent resistance had reached its limits. You were not yet a month old when the moral geography of the anti-apartheid struggle was permanently altered.

**Seventy Days Later: The Pill**

On May 9, 1960 — seventy days after your birth — the United States Food and Drug Administration approved the first oral contraceptive. Enovid, manufactured by G.D. Searle & Company, became the first drug approved not to treat a disease but to prevent a natural biological process. The implications were vast and contested and slow to fully unfold, but they did unfold: within five years, millions of American women were using it; within a decade, it had reshaped the social architecture of marriage, work, medicine, and reproductive autonomy in ways that touched nearly every life in the Western world. The generation born in your year grew up alongside it and came of age in the world it helped make.

**The Spy Plane Summer**

Two months after your birth, on May 1, 1960, an American U-2 reconnaissance aircraft was shot down over the Soviet Union. The pilot, Francis Gary Powers, survived and was captured. The Eisenhower administration initially denied the flight had any intelligence purpose; the Soviets produced Powers and the wreckage. The lie collapsed. A planned summit between Eisenhower and Khrushchev was canceled. The Cold War, which had seemed to be entering a cautious thaw, snapped back into hard frost. You were three months old when the framework of superpower diplomacy cracked in public view over the skies of central Russia.

**The Man Running for President**

In February 1960, John F. Kennedy was 42 years old and running hard for the Democratic presidential nomination. He had announced his candidacy in January, was campaigning through the primary states, and was making the argument — quietly, to the right audiences — that his Catholicism should not disqualify him from the presidency. The question of whether America would elect a Catholic president had been answered once, in 1928, with a resounding no. Kennedy was making the bet that the country had changed. By November, he would win the presidency by a margin of roughly 100,000 popular votes out of nearly 69 million cast, and the question would be settled. He was inaugurated when you were ten months old.

**The Year of Africa, from the Beginning**

1960 is called the Year of Africa. Seventeen nations on the continent gained independence that single year — more than in any comparable period before or since. The process had been set in motion by years of anti-colonial organizing and by Britain's explicit acknowledgment, in Harold Macmillan's "Wind of Change" speech the week before your birth, that European empire in Africa was ending. You were born at the hinge. The map of Africa in 1959 and the map of Africa in 1961 are recognizably different documents.

**Sixty-Six Years**

You are 66 years old. You were born in a year that approved the birth control pill, launched the first weather satellite, filmed *Psycho*, and produced *To Kill a Mockingbird*. You were nine when humans walked on the moon. You were 20 when Ronald Reagan was elected and the political axis of your adulthood tilted. You were 29 when the Wall fell, 31 when the Soviet Union dissolved, 41 on September 11th. You have watched the internet arrive, the smartphone become indispensable, and now artificial intelligence reshape the terms of thought and work.

---

You were born a leap day child into a night when a Moroccan city was being buried, three weeks before Sharpeville changed South Africa, ten weeks before the birth control pill was approved, and in the year that more of the African continent gained independence than in any other. It was not a quiet entry. Leap day 1960 arrived in a world already moving fast, already breaking from its old arrangements — and you have had sixty-six years of watching what those breaks eventually became.
